Was The Suspect Really Wearing Louboutins?: An Examination of Character Usage Across Different Sources
We’ve all dreamt about being rich and famous, right? If you said no, stop lying. If you said yes, I imagine you understand the appeal of lavish clothes, mansions, and attention from the media. This is especially true in modern times, when we have the best examples of the lifestyles we think we deserve at the tips of our fingers. With a click of a remote or a swipe on a phone screen, we can see what famous people are doing, how, where, and with whom. With such easy access, it’s rare not to fall into the trap of comparison, which can be especially devastating for the ones with the short end of the stick like us. But just how far would you go to be one of them? To dress like them, eat like them, live like them? To answer this question, take a look at this case study.
In 2008, a group of affluent teenagers from Los Angeles stole over 3 million dollars in clothes, bags, weapons, jewelry, and cash from celebrity’s homes. Some of these celebrities included Rachel Bilson, Audrina Partridge, Orlando Bloom, and perhaps most notoriously, Paris Hilton (Sales). When questions in regard to their motives, they all had a cohesive answer: their obsession with celebrities. They admired their lifestyles, mannerisms, styles, and most importantly, their notoriety. 
Ironically enough, by committing these crimes, they became famous too. The best example of this is Alexis Neiers, the daughter of a former Playboy bunny and aspiring model (Sales). Given her unique profile, she was placed front and center in the media coverage, even though she wasn’t as involved as others in the ring. The reasons to why they did this remains unknown, but it has been speculated that outlets used her personal brand to personify the nature of the crimes. This can be clearly evidenced in two of the central media depictions of these crimes: Nancy Jo Sales’ Vanity Fair article "The Suspects Wore Louboutins" and Sofia Coppola’s 2013 film adaptation The Bling Ring. This raises the question: how does the usage of Alexis Neiers as a character affect the narrative surrounding the crimes in the film and article?

In “The Suspects Wore Louboutins”, Alexis Neiers is placed front and center, literally being on the cover page of the article (Sales). The events are mostly narrated through her point of view, mostly in quotations, but Sales constantly diminishes Alexis’s credibility with microaggressions. A great example of this is when the events of the first robbery were being discussed, and Sales quotes Alexis saying “‘[w]hat are you doing? Get me the fuck out of here,’ Neiers said she screamed. Then she went outside and threw up and peed in the bushes” (2010). Instead of simply quoting Alexis, or stating the events, Sales uses a combination of both, with the addition of a ‘said she screamed’. This gives the readers the idea that Alexis’s words are not credible, especially with her state of inebriation being clarified in the next sentence. 
In addition to this, Sales uses specific things that Alexis says to further the idea that she is just a dumb teenager, like when she was quoted saying “God didn’t give me these talents and looks to just sit around being a model or being famous. I want to lead a huge charity organization. I want to lead a country, for all I know” (Sales). This is the only quote like this in the entire article, as no other characters were quoted saying such things, which selectively sheds light on the type of person Alexis is. Moreover, Sales even goes as far as to pit the kid’s words against each other, which can be seen when she quotes Nick Prugo, another one of the suspects, denying Alexis’s first ever statement in the article by saying, “Nick Prugo has a different take on the events of the night of the Bloom burglary. ‘We didn’t even go to Beso that night,’…” (Sales). This, specifically, accomplishes two things: it takes even more credibility from Alexis, and it makes the kids seem disorganized and stupid as a whole. 
Not only that, but Sales uses the acknowledgement of small aesthetic details to further her superficial depiction of Alexis. This can be seen starting from the title of the article, as it emphasizes the kid’s wealth by mentioning a luxury brand. This can also be seen when Sales’ first describes Alexis going into court, saying she was a “A leggy girl with long, dark hair and shimmering blue-green eyes, Neiers was wearing a tweed miniskirt, a pink sweater, and six-inch Christian Louboutin heels” (Sales). In the anniversary article, Sales describes how she mentioned Neiers’s shoes and other luxury items, which she felt were justified in a story centered on celebrity and consumerism (Sales). This approach illustrates how details, like designer shoes, reinforce an image of wealth and superficiality in media, which could supports the idea of the media’s power to shape public perception through specific choices in portrayal. Besides from the fact that this makes Alexis look bad, it was later disproven in a phone call between her and Sales as shown in her show Pretty Wild, where she says that “[Sales] said I was wearing six-inch Louboutins to court with my tweed outfit. I wasn’t wearing Louboutins, I was wearing little brown kitten heels fucking bitch” (Vanity fair, 2013). 
By doing these sorts of things throughout the article, Sales solidifies the idea that Alexis is a spoiled, superficial, dumb teenager. Not only that, but also that Alexis was the front-runner of the ring. In the context of these crimes, being portrayed as superficial, disorganized, and unreliable—as Sales suggests Alexis is—is devastating, as these were precisely the perceptions the kids aimed to counter to mitigate both their social and judicial sentences. David L. Bruce, from the Department of Learning and Instruction at SUNY Buffalo, provides insight on how teenagers are culturally constructed and stereotyped in media, which eerily aligns with Alexis’s case. More specifically, Bruce says that “[m]edia portrayals of adolescents often reflect and reinforce societal stereotypes, reducing them to superficial characteristics that align with cultural constructs of fame, rebellion, and irresponsibility” (Bruce). In the article, Sales’ selective quoting and editorial choices feed into the “spoiled airhead” narrative, further exemplifying Bruce’s point about media’s tendency to oversimplify and stereotype teens.
In the film, however, Alexis isn’t a main character. The plot mostly revolves around Nick and Rachel, their drug use, the reason they commit the crimes, and how they did it. For context, Nick and Rachel, called Marc and Rebecca in the film, were the two ‘ringleaders’, with Rebecca being the one initiating all the robberies, and Nick always standing by her side. In a way, this aligns with the article, as Nick’s point of view is also constantly shared, and their depictions of him align with one another. Alexis’s lack of centrality in the film better reflects the real succession of events, and the fact that the true ringleaders were Nick and Rachel. Alexis, Tess, and the other kids were just tagging along.  This shift in focus from Alexis to Nick and Rachel is crucial to the added depth, as Nick and Rachel’s stories have much more to offer than Alexis’s.
Coppola also constantly makes it known that these crimes were done out of boredom and greed, but that these characters are still people. She does this by highlighting their struggles instead of their flaws. This can be evidenced by the emphasis placed on Mark (Nick)’s ostracism at school and Rebecca (Rachel)’s problems with her parents, and how the characters suffered as a result. In addition to this, the film shows how drugs influenced the crimes, which ended up being a lot, as many of the kids were borderline addicts at the time of the crimes (Sales). 
Moreover, Coppola takes great care in making the film falsely seem superficial, having short clip lengths, accentuating material items, using real name brands, and a painfully 2009’s LA script. But she places this in combination with the demonstrations of the kid’s personal lives and struggles, which effectively make the crimes feel more meaningful than in the article.  This is supported by Sales’ commentary of the film in the 10-year anniversary article titled “Exclusive: Nancy Jo Sales on the 10th Anniversary of the Bling Ring”, saying “[i]t was [not] a shallow film, instead of a film about the shallowness of our era” (Sales). 
These pieces, however different, provide a similar baseline understanding of the crimes to the audience. At the end of the day, there wasn’t really much to it: just a bunch of rich kids getting bored and stealing from celebrities after looking up their information online. Even though Sales’s usage of Alexis gives the crimes a sense of idiocy and superficiality, Coppola’s lack-there-of also accomplishes the same thing, just differently. The film clarifies the idea that while, these robberies were all about celebrity culture and materialism, the people who committed them were still, well, people. This, in turn, slightly changes the tone of these narratives; the article is more bubbly, while the film is much deeper. Subsequently, this changes the ambiance of the crimes. Both the article and the film use Neiers differently to explore themes of fame and materialism, but with distinct tones—Sales presenting her as emblematic of superficiality, and Coppola as part of a larger cultural obsession. While the depiction of the events is pretty much the same in both, this small but significant shift in the film makes it understood that this is more than just a cover story, but a real life succession of events. 
Some can argue that both the article and the film accurately reflect Alexis and the other kids, claiming they embody the stereotype of spoiled, celebrity-obsessed teenagers. They might even say that Sales' portrayal is just honest reporting, showing Alexis as she presented herself: shallow, lacking self-awareness, and materialistic. To them, the film only emphasizes these traits through its aesthetic choices, short clips, and carefully constructed dialogue, reflecting culture rather than a stereotype. If examined through this perspective, Alexis wasn't a victim of media manipulation—she was simply being herself.
However, to accept this argument ignores the specific framing that both Sales and Coppola used to create a specific narrative. Sales chose certain quotes and moments while downplaying other perspectives and critical aspects of Alexis's story. Similarly, Coppola's film, though not centered on Alexis, uses cliched, exaggerated aesthetics to frame the entire group as one-dimensional caricatures of youth, rather than as complex people with motivations and struggles. 
In the end, the portrayals of Alexis Neiers in “The Suspects Wore Louboutins” and “The Bling Ring” reveal how cultural constructs and media choices shape our perceptions of events and of people. Nancy Jo Sales’ article leans into a superficial, critical portrayal, using Alexis as the symbol of shallow, fame-driven youth, while Sofia Coppola’s film subtly explores the underlying social and personal struggles without putting Alexis in the spotlight. These contrasting approaches echo David L. Bruce’s insights on media’s power to reinforce stereotypes, often reducing real people to caricatures to create compelling narratives. By comparing the article’s focus on Alexis’s carefully constructed persona with the film’s broader depiction of teenagers and their angst, we see how these media shapes selectively frame stories to fit cultural expectations.

Reproductive success is defined by anthropologists and evolutionary biologists as the ability to pass one’s genes onto the next generation. Across mammals, this success is influenced and limited by factors that mostly depend on gender, which leads to distinct reproductive strategies across the two. In humans, the influence of this evolutionary pressure is pretty obvious, and it has been heavily affected by social, cultural, and technological advances humanity has recently made. This essay aims to explore how reproductive limitations shape behaviors across mammals, and seeing how it applies to humans. With this in mind, it will then examine the basis for human mating motivations, addressing the naturalistic fallacy and discussing the relevance of environmental mismatch in the modern context. 
As aforementioned, reproductive success limitations vary by gender in mammals. This is defined by the fact that, as a minimum, males only have to contribute sperm for reproduction, while females have to become pregnant and then feed the child for the first few months of its life. This makes it so that the reproductive success of males is limited by their access to mates, while the reproductive success of females is limited by their access to the resources required for gestation and weaning. As a result, females typically produce fewer offspring over their lifetime compared to males. 
This clearly shows up in the differing mating strategies of each gender. Seeing as they have fewer opportunities to pass on their genes, female mammals have to focus on finding high quality mates that will increase the probability of survival of the offspring. Because of this, they are more selective, often choosing the more physically fit and dominant males over any others. In addition to this, they can further increase their offspring’s chance at survival by selecting a mate that will offer parental investment. 
Males, on the other hand, prioritize finding as many mating opportunities as possible. This shows up in the fact that males often court multiple females at once. Furthermore, seeing as females have higher standards, males have to compete with one another for these opportunities, which can show up directly, as physical confrontations and displays of dominance, or through sexual dimorphism. This can include the development of features like antlers, manes, or vibrant coloration to attract females. In species where females are more selective, be it because of higher base levels of parental investment or other reasons, sexual dimorphism is higher. An example of this is peacocks, and how the male bird has a beautiful, vibrant plumage, while the female is brown and dull (Kostarakos et al., 2008). This is supported by Dominic Edward and Tracey Chapman, from the School of Biological Sciences of the University of East Anglia as they highlight that “Sex differences in the evolution of mate choice were originally attributed to variation in parental investment between males and females” (2011), and by Michael Jennions and Marion Petrie from the Department of Zoology at Oxford, who argue that, “Increased choosiness by females can influence the evolution of male secondary sexual characteristics” (1997). 
Top put this all together, let’s explore an example. Female elephants live in matriarchal groups and invest heavily in raising calves for years. They prioritize long-term investment in calf survival by relying on social bonds within their matriarchal herd. Conversely, male elephants are solitary. They are free to roam in search of mating opportunities, often resulting in competition with other males for access to females. Mature males periodically enter a condition called musth, which is characterized by higher testosterone levels, aggression, and sexual activity. But although males compete, the final choice lies with the female, who tends to go with males who demonstrate superior physical traits or dominance, ensuring strong genetics for their offspring.
 While humans share many biological imperatives with other animals, differing evolutionary developments have shaped our mating strategies to best fit our needs. As humans developed bipedalism, the female’s pelvis (and birth canal) had to become smaller, which, in combination with the evolution of larger brains, resulted in newborns having to be born almost completely helpless (Edward & Chapman, 2011). This made it so that there is an extended period of dependence during childhood. Larger brains then enabled more complex social behaviors, problem-solving, and communication. This led to the development of cultural and social norms that influence mate selection, parenting, and familial structures, such as monogamy and polygyny. Now let’s explore the specifics. 
Similar to most other mammals, female humans invest more heavily in reproduction, which then affects their mate selection strategies. As in other female mammals, this makes them more selective, often opting for men that show physical fitness, intelligence, and dominance, but also traits like high social status, reliability, fidelity, and kindness. Studies show that women prefer more masculine traits (good genes) during ovulation, but value resource-based traits (investment) when considering long-term partners. By selecting a male with these traits, they can increase the chance that their mate helps them get the necessary resources to successfully raise a child, and also that the child is fit enough to reproduce itself. To support this, Eduard and Chapman note that “Mutual mate choice is observed in species exhibiting biparental care, which aligns with human tendencies for long-term pair bonding” (CITE). In addition to this, humans rely on social groups for child-rearing, typically depending on other people to help take care of their child. While this isn’t very common amongst mammals, it has been observed, with elephants being an example. 
Human males, like their mammal counterparts, can father multiple offspring with little investment, leading to behaviors that increase mating opportunities, like searching for mates with high reproductive potential. This shows up in many ways, an example being the unchanging mate age preference of males, and how it directly relates to the female’s peak in reproductive age. Additionally, studies show that males tend to prefer traits that signal youth and fertility, such as clear skin and an optimal waist-to-hip ratio. Not only that, but human males also engage in mate competition, though this usually takes non-physical forms, like achieving status, wealth, or social influence. Still, human males display levels of investment mostly unseen in other animals, often engaging in lifelong pair bonding with one female. In humans specifically, investing in kids can help ensure their survival, and therefore the inheritance of their genes to the next generation. More concretely, this is called cooperative parenting, and is likely due to the uncommonly long childhood dependency that human kids have, and how they require more resources after being born than other animals. However, they also evolved to value traits that ensure their investment isn’t wasted on non-biological offspring (Jennions & Petrie, 1997).
        Moreover, evolved motivational systems affect the ways humans mate, working to maximize reproductive success. Romantic love, for example, fosters emotional bonds and commitment. This encourages long-term partnerships, which are beneficial for cooperative parenting and ensuring offspring survival. On the other hand, jealousy guards against the loss of a mate’s investment in females, but guards against infidelity to ensure paternity certainty in males. Motivational systems as such have helped humans successfully reproduce to the best of their ability, fostering behaviors that increase reproductive success and offspring survival.

When examining evolutionary bases for mating behavior, it is easy to fall into the trap of the naturalistic fallacy. This may show up in many forms, including the perpetuation of gender stereotypes. Someone can easily argue that as women invest more, they are meant to be at home with their kids instead of working and having a career. This is wrong because in the modern environment, women can do both, and that choice has very little to do with our biology. Additionally, in this context, the naturalistic fallacy can show up when justifying cheating. For example, a person might argue that since evolution has shaped males to seek more than one partner to maximize reproductive success, cheating is acceptable. This reasoning is erroneous on the grounds that while seeking multiple partners may have been advantageous for our ancestors, it does not justify damaging a committed relationship today. Edward and Chapman support this, saying that “Understanding the origins of behavior does not equate to moral justification for those behaviors”​ (2011). 
Seeing as the environment has drastically changed from the one we evolved in, there is bound to be mismatch between our evolved mating systems and the current milieu. An example of this environmental change is the development of technology, and how mate-finding has been reduced to swiping right or left on apps like Tinder, Bumble, or Hinge. As a result, it is very easy for people to lie about their identity and other things that would make potential mates choose them. In addition to this, the sheer amount of mate choices now available to us, unthinkable in the ancestral environment, could lead to “choice overload” and superficial decision-making. This can then result in reduced satisfaction with partners due to constant access to alternative options (“the grass is always greener” effect) and diminished emphasis on building deep connections. Before, humans knew about 200 people in their entire lifetime (Jennions & Petrie, 1997). The dating pool was small, and choices were easy. Nowadays, the dating pool set up by social media is too large, creating confusion, but mostly unnecessarily increasing competition in the search for mates. Continuing upon that, humans have developed many methods of fooling cues of youth and fertility, such as makeup, plastic surgery, and online filters. These can trick others into picking people they wouldn’t otherwise go for, therefore skewing mate selection. Additionally, it can set up unrealistic expectations for people looking for mates, making it harder to form lasting relationships. Moreover, the creation of contraception has separated sexual behavior from reproduction (Kostarakos et al., 2008). This leads to a greater emphasis on casual relationships, which can conflict with people’s desire for long-term commitment or general intimacy, which we have evolved to prefer. Finally, seeing as modern society has mostly been built around the traditional family structure, there is much more pressure for people to conform to this, altering behaviors to fit the norm. All of this mismatch can result in feelings of isolation, loneliness, and a general decrease in mental health.

As explored in this essay, reproductive success is a critical driver of behavior across species, shaped by evolutionary pressures and environmental contexts throughout time. In mammals, these behaviors are deeply influenced by gender, and the unique limitations it comes with, having females typically prioritizing quality of mates and males prioritizing quantity of mates. This becomes more evident when specific species are examined, from peacocks to elephants and even humans providing evidence for this. More specifically, evolved human reproductive strategies are also subject to modern influences, such as technology and culture. The interplay between evolutionary adaptations and environmental changes can lead to mismatches, exemplified by modern dating apps and altered social structures. This demonstrates the true complexity of applying evolutionary theory to today’s human behaviors. However, while biology informs behavior, it does not dictate the ethical or social norms of human society.

Final Reflective Essay
Although my time at BU has been short, I have been able to tremendously grow my writing abilities through the writing curriculum and other classes. Even though I had a lot of experience with academic writing, seeing as I took all the AP English courses in high school (Lang, Lit, Seminar, and Research), I began feeling a bit unsure of my bases in the first semester at WR120. It took me a while to regain my footing by purposefully changing the way in which I was approaching writing, and also by making a greater effort to provide quality work. This, in turn, helped me in other classes I was taking at the time that also required writing. By the time I got to the second semester, I felt much more confident in my skills, and know that I’m a much better writer than I originally was. Additionally, WR153 has helped me strengthen my voice as a writer, helping my develop my own style based on my taste and preferences. Although this may not be as important in purely academic writing, it will definitively be helpful when I write for anything outside of class, be it for myself or for other projects. This way, I can make my writing my own. Additionally, the fact that I took two courses that related film with literature greatly helped me in connecting writing to the real world continually and in many ways. Because of these courses, I grew greatly fond of literary-themed movies, and also film adaptations of literature in general. This has expanded my taste, which I appreciate immensely.

To trace my growth, I want to start with the WR120 assignment I chose to feature. In that essay, I analyzed how a single character was portrayed in both a Vanity Fair article and its film adaptation. The article, The Suspects Wore Louboutins, covered a string of celebrity home burglaries in the early 2000s. Sofia Coppola later adapted the piece into a film, drawing heavily from the article. The character I focused on was Alexis Neiers, as she was pinpointed as one of the ringleaders simply because she made an interesting character, regardless of her actual involvement in the crimes. In order to delve into this, I had to bring in an external academic source, for which I selected a journal article about teen stereotypes in the media. In the end, I feel like I did a good job exploring this topic. It truly interested me, which greatly helped to motivate me to produce good work. This comes to show how I tend to write better when the topics I write about actually matter to me, and also helped me understand that I truly enjoy writing about modern media. Additionally, the feedback I got on this paper, be it though my peers or the professor, really helped me refine my skills in writing about more contemporary topics, as I was used to writing about heavier, more academic topics.

Simultaneously, I was taking CASAN 234, a course about evolutionary anthropology. I absolutely loved this class, and greatly enjoyed writing all the papers doing the readings. Because of this, when it came to writing about reproductive success, I was golden. Using the skills I was developing in WR120, I was able to produce what I believe to be a really good research paper. I was able to relate the ancestral environment to modern times with ease, which I doubt I’d be able to do with the writing skills I had before I came to college. This is why I chose to include it as my featured writing piece for outside WR writing.

Finally, I’d like to talk about my WR153 work. This course has been my favorite by far, so the work I’ve produced has really come easily to me. As I said in my process paper for the anthology, I didn’t like poetry before signing up for the class, but slowly developed a certain fondness for it as the course progressed. The usage of Dickinson, Bishop, and Plath “... helped me see poetry as more than just words on paper, but rather parts of real people’s souls” (Reflection 3, WR153). As I read more, grew familiar with poetry, and honed my analytical skills, I became a stronger poet—which is why I chose to feature a piece I wrote for this class. It’s one I wrote towards the end as an imitation of Bishop’s Geography II, as I feel it displays my newfound skills best.

Looking back, I’m grateful for how much these courses have pushed me—not just to write better, but to think more sharply and choose topics that matter to me. They’ve made writing feel less like a task and more like a tool I can use, whether I’m breaking down a film, exploring scientific ideas, or shaping a poem. With these courses, I’ve learned to trust my instincts, revise with intention, and let my voice come through, even when the subject is academic. More than anything, I leave these classes knowing that my writing is mine now—something I can carry into any space, academic or not, with clarity, confidence, and care.

Mapping a Taste: Learning to Love Poetry on My Own Terms

If I’m being completely honest, I didn’t really like poetry before this semester. It was a foreign land I didn’t know how to traverse, and didn’t think I could learn how. Each time I read a poem I didn’t understand, I found the idea of poetry increasingly less appealing. Many of my closest friends—who often feel like extensions of me—are poetry lovers, constantly explaining their references. My high school English teacher, whom I deeply respect, always urged me to explore poetry on my own. And most of the people I admire seem somehow connected to it. All of that made me feel like there had to be something more to poetry than what I’d seen so far, and I wanted to know what it was. Then, during course registration, I saw my window of opportunity and signed up for this class. As the course progressed and I got to know different forms and voices—like Plath’s intensity in “Daddy”, or the precision of Bishop’s “The Fish” (Plath 222; Bishop 42)—I finally began to find meaning in what I was reading. And with that, I started to like it. Then I came across a quote on my Instagram feed: “We don’t like what we can’t fully understand”. Although I don’t fully agree, the quote resonates with me. I think of how lost I felt reading Plath’s “Lady Lazarus” for the first time, or how Bishop’s “One Art” seemed cold until I reread it and finally heard the grief beneath the restraint (Plath 245; Bishop 327). Those moments showed me how poetry can unfold slowly, revealing more the longer you sit with it. My early resistance wasn’t genuine dislike, but rather a distance to it.
The exploration of the poets Emily Dickinson, Elizabeth Bishop, and Sylvia Plath was a great way of getting me into poetry in the first place, as they showed me the range that exists within poetry. From Dickinson’s cryptic exploration of nature and relationships to Bishop’s travel diaries and to Plath’s eccentric interpretations of life, I gathered that there is much to see in poetry. Still, seeing that they were all tied to Massachusetts was interesting, as the thought of all of them being connected like that was something that helped me understand some underlying parts of poetry. 
Additionally, the fact that we got to explore the lives of these poets through film made them seem more approachable. Although some film adaptations of their lives were not my taste (Dickinson the TV show), others were (Reaching For the Moon and Sylvia). The important thing was that they helped me see poetry as more than just words on paper, but rather parts of real people’s souls. They had lives, in the same way that I have a life, and they used their experiences as fuel for their writing, however different they were from each other. This inspired me to start writing my own poetry. 
In building my anthology, I decided that I was going to keep the theme primal, per se. I didn’t want to restrict myself to something concrete, say a theme or a certain interpretation of the poems. Furthermore, I feel that I connect to poetry unconventionally. Instead of understanding or deriving meaning and connecting to that, I focus on how the poem makes me feel. While sometimes I do find myself drawn to the meaning, I often enjoy poems whose words or ambiance I like. I understand how this may seem abstract, but I’ll delve into it later in the paper with illustrative examples. Although I haven't been able to distinguish what the poems I like have in common, I do know that they are the ones I just connect with, and that is enough for me. This is why I made my anthology a collection of poems I simply feel drawn to, however abstract that is. Hopefully, as it changes and grows, I’ll be able to identify what these poems have in common, and use that in my own writing.
Starting with Dickinson was rough. At first, her writing seemed too abstract. I constantly found myself reaching for the craziest meanings simply to make the words on the page make sense. She often talked about death and nature, both things that I know, but am not close to. Moreover, the way that she talked about death was too foreign to me; she welcomed it like an old friend. Still, I was able to learn to appreciate the way in which she perceived the world around her. Not only that, but the way she chose to depict it in her writing. While her life was completely different to mine, which would ordinarily make it harder for me to connect with her writing, I was still able to find poems of hers that I wanted to include in my anthology. A good example of this is “The heart asks pleasure first”, and how it goes through the stages of attempting to escape pain, only to surrender to its inevitability (Dickinson 376). I don’t feel that way now, but I’ve known the weight of that hopelessness—when suffering seems inescapable and the only imagined release is to stop feeling altogether. Dickinson’s final turn—“And then—to go to sleep— / And then—the Second step / We do not wish to know—”—captures that resignation with chilling grace. Of course, it made the cut. On the other hand, another poem I included was “As Sleigh Bells seem in Summer” (Dickinson 402). I first chose it for the memorization assignment because it sounded good—I liked the way the rhythm moved, how the lines flickered. Reading it aloud, I loved the way “As Sleigh Bells seem in Summer / Or Bees, at Christmas show—” felt surreal and precise. Only later, with help from the internet and some rereading, I uncovered how deeply I connected to its themes—the fragility of presence, the unreliability of what we think is real. That confusion, then clarity, mirrored my experience with much of Dickinson. But what pulled me in first was the structure—the music in her form—and that’s why it stayed with me. These examples illustrate my process with Dickinson’s poetry, and how, although I may not immediately understand the content, I can enjoy her writing through other means. 
Next, we covered Bishop. Her life, as we learned in the biographies and films, was marked by loss, constant travel, and a quiet kind of exile. I cannot relate to any of that on a personal level, as I haven’t experienced much loss, have travelled but not as extensively, and have never known that kind of solitude or dislocation. But her poetry felt more accessible than Dickinson’s. Bishop observes the world precisely while holding back her emotions, a style that aligns more with the writing I’ve grown up reading: structured, descriptive, grounded in the external. In “The Fish”, for example, she builds the moment detail by detail—the “rainbow” of oil in the water, the “coarse white flesh packed in like feathers”—until meaning surfaces almost accidentally (Bishop 42). That methodical unfolding made her feel easier to understand, not because the emotions were simpler, but because she leads the reader to them through the physical aesthetics rather than asking them to feel them upfront, as Dickinson often does. This simplified the whole meaning-abstraction process, as it decreased the need for constant dictionary consults and ultra-close reading, which helped me build my poetry analysis skills from the basics. However, this is not to say that Bishop’s content is by any means “simple”, or “unsophisticated”, but rather that I could go straight to the point without having to remove all the fluff as I was used to. This being said, I really enjoyed the subjects and themes of these poems, as I was able to connect with them much more easily. I’ve always loved travelling and the outdoors, which I Bishop clearly has a mastery over. I also enjoyed how casually she talks about emotions like loss and love, as her exploration of them was new to me. Additionally, her straightforward language and clean structure gave the poems a casual tone, which made them feel less intimidating. I don’t know if it’s her personality, her voice, or just the way she frames experience, but I found myself connecting with her work more easily than I did with Dickinson’s—regardless of the topic. Because of that connection, choosing which of her poems to include in my anthology felt natural, even obvious.
Finally, we delved into Plath. She was the poet I was most familiar with, and my favorite by far. I already knew I liked her work, so I took this as an opportunity to understand her as a person, which really helped me in analyzing her poems. I like how directly reflected her life is on her work, as it adds depth and meaning. A great example of this is “Nick and the Candlestick”, which she wrote after she gave birth to her son (Plath 205). Without context, the poem seems daunting and complicated, but once you know what it’s about, it makes much more sense. Moreover, I love the raw nature of her poetry, however controversial it may be. In a way, I understand why she chose to include such harsh features in her work; she felt everything very deeply, and needed to convey it. In “Daddy”, for instance, she compares her father to a Nazi and herself to a Jew, an incendiary and radical way to characterize a situation (Plath 222). But then again, the whole poem is about her struggle to break free from the psychological grip of her father—and, more broadly, from patriarchal authority and inherited trauma, so maybe she deemed strong language necessary. While I don’t relate to many of the poems she wrote, seeing as they were written in the face of hyperspecific situations, I do appreciate her writing. “Heavy Woman”, “Daddy”, “Mirror”, and “Love Letter”, are all poems that I can’t personally relate to, but thoroughly enjoyed reading for their style (Plath 219, 222, 173, 188). On the other hand, I felt deeply seen by Sylvia Plath while getting to know her work. Some examples of this are “The Fearful” and “Miss Drake Proceeds to Supper” (Plath 200, 198). Specifically, I never really knew how I felt about motherhood until I read the poem and had an almost visceral reaction to it. 
Based upon my newly gathered knowledge about poetry, I then built the miscellaneous part of my anthology. I knew that I wanted to read Bukowski, as I’d always wanted to get into his work, but never really got the chance. To do this, I recruited a friend who is a big Bukowski fan, and whom I relate to profoundly, and asked her to give advice on where to start. She gave me around 30 poems to read, from which I chose my 5 favorite. Although the anthology is supposed to be uniquely “mine”, I think incorporating the taste of the ones we love makes the process more personal. Surprisingly, I found myself relating to Bukowski much more than with any of the aforementioned poets. Although our lives have virtually no overlap, I think our minds work similarly, as I felt very understood by much of what I read. The best examples of this are “The Tragedy of the Leaves” and “Bluebird” (Bukowski, Love 9; Fire 88). I almost cried when I read them because it was shocking to see my feelings put on paper in such a beautiful way. With “Bluebird” especially, I realized there is a part of me I suppress in order to protect it, but also that I’m not the only one that feels that way. For the rest of the poems, I included poetry that I remembered from different stages of my life. The sole fact that I remembered a poem makes it special to me, but I still filtered the ones I cared for the most. “The Two-Headed Calf” by Linda Pastan, “Universal Truths” by Shira Haus (Elrichman), and “This Is Just to Say” by William Carlos Williams (Pastan 76; Erlichman; Williams 336) all made it. These are poems I remember discovering organically. They weren’t assigned, and no one pushed me toward them. That makes them personal.

As for my own poems, I chose the ones I actually felt proud of. I liked having guiding prompts, especially the imitation ones, as they really helped me refine what I needed to write. Having an example I was supposed to follow really made the process easier, which I feel helped enormously with writer's block. The poem that came easiest was “Spring Break”, as I had Bishop’s poem as a template to fill out with my own experience. My favorite out the poems I wrote was “Where the Leash First Loosened” because it is based on my personal experience. Although the subject of the poem isn’t as serious as others we’ve covered, I liked writing something that felt so personal to me. 
All in all, the making of this anthology helped me feel closer to poetry, which motivated me to continue reading, and hopefully make it one day. Although I haven’t quite figured out the underlying patterns that show up in the things I like, having a collection of work I truly love feels like a beginning — a reminder that poetry can be personal, spontaneous, and still grow alongside me. Knowing this, I feel more motivated to keep reading, writing, and exploring what poetry has to offer. If time and circumstance ever allow, I would love to follow in Plath’s footsteps and write a collection of my own, something raw and alive like The Colossus.

Watching the Voices & Visions documentary on Sylvia Plath shifted the way I think about literary research. I’d always assumed “sources” meant books, essays, archives—things you could underline, cite, or footnote. But director Lawrence Pitkethly and writer Susan Yankowitz did something else entirely for this film; a living archive. Their portrait of Plath is constructed not through argument as biographies often are, but through accumulation. There is more to Plath than just her biographical facts, which they explore in the intersection between multiple sources, all nuanced and specific in their own way. This creates the complex and comprehensive depiction this documentary offers. 
The end product of this type of research is what can best be described as a mosaic, with each testimony, fact, and media serving as the pieces that make the picture. A great example of this is the testimonies that the producers chose to include; her mother Aurelia’s clipped resolve, Al Alvarez’s raw recollections, or Anne Stevenson’s conflicted admiration. Alvarez says Plath was “exhilarated by the edge of things,” and the film takes him seriously; there’s always an edge, whether it’s a thin line of horizon under a blood-orange sky or the sharp break in her voice reading Lady Lazarus. Pitkethly overlays beauty and menace with deliberate tension, creating a framework of sorts for the way Plath lived—lit up, undone, controlled, unraveling.
The script doesn’t flatten Plath into a cautionary tale or a martyr, which is easy to do with a person as complex as her. Instead, it lets her remain sharp, ambitious, and simultaneously, perfectly self-aware. The film suggests she wasn’t just writing from pain, but with it, using it almost as an instrument. Although the filmmakers make it clear that she suffered, they also make it clear that it sculpted her into the person, and therefore, writer she became, which is a really important thing to understand when analyzing her work. 
I left the film thinking that Plath was both a construct and a creator, myth and woman, speaking through the frame even as others tried to claim it. Additionally, it made me reconsider my concept of evidence in academic settings. Maybe it’s not just what’s written down in a dusty book somewhere, or in a peer-reviewed database. Maybe it’s voice. Image. Omission. A camera lingering one second too long. A hesitation in a mother’s smile. It’s all part of the archive, and more importantly, all part of her work.

Throughout the semester, this course has helped me develop intellectually and personally through the exploration of how anthropology and evolution shape human behavior. But out of everything, two of the central topics of the course really stuck with me: the evolved motivational system of emotions and the reproductive strategies of humans. By examining these areas, I’ve not only gained an academic understanding of them, but developed tools that have helped me understand myself and others better, while also getting a better grasp on group dynamics and society.

In the first part of the course, and our first essay, we explored motivational systems, and how they operate through specialized triggers and responses that prepare individuals to act in adaptive ways. More particularly, we delved into how these helped our ancestors survive in the EEA by shaping their behavior, and continue to do so to this day. For example, emotions that drive individuals to seek safety, avoid threats, or restore social connections kept our ancestors alive long enough for them to reproduce and pass on these motivational systems to their offspring. While these responses were essential in the EEA, modern environments often present mismatches that complicate them. Now, factors like technology, urbanization, and social media can alter the inputs that trigger these motivational systems. While these emotions used to guide us to act in certain ways, like avoiding physical threats or keeping close social bonds, the same mechanisms might now lead to persistent negative states when those actions are no longer effective. Understanding the evolutionary roots of my emotions have helped me see them more objectively, therefore helping me manage them more easily. Additionally, this has made me more empathetic. Recognizing that emotions have evolved to serve us encouraged me to have a more compassionate view of behaviors that could otherwise seem irrational or overly reactive.
In the second essay we wrote, we explored the reproductive strategies of humans and evolutionary mating systems. In class and in my independent research, I found that the most important concept in this topic is how the differences in reproductive success factors between males and females across mammals really change mating strategies. In mammals specifically, males are reproductively limited to their access to mates, while females are limited by gestation and caregiving demands. This leads females to prioritize mate quality over quantity, limiting males and increasing competition. These evolutionary pressures manifest in humans with unique twists due to cultural and biological evolution.
For example, humans show an unusually high degree of paternal investment, which has shaped both sexes to value long-term relationships and cooperation when it comes to parenting. Still, differences in mate preference remain. Women tend to prefer traits that signal skill at resource acquisition and stability, while men prefer fertility cues. With these strategies, women can find good quality mates, while men can reproduce more successfully. 
The modern environment, though, complicates this dynamic, as technology and culture play a large role in today’s mating landscape. A few examples of these game-changers include dating apps, the family structure, and contraception. These all create an increase in priority of superficial traits, unrealistic expectations, and choice overload. Perhaps most notoriously, this has created the separation of sex from reproduction. Reflecting on these mismatches has deepened my understanding of contemporary relationship struggles, allowing me to approach these issues in my own life and others’ with greater empathy.
One of the most challenging, but rewarding, parts of this course was learning about the naturalistic fallacy. It has always been tempting for me to justify behaviors like jealousy or loneliness as “natural” and, therefore, acceptable, but this is wrong, as it oversimplifies evolutionary theory and ignores any ethical considerations. 
For example, a girl might justify being toxic in her relationship because being jealous is an ‘evolved’ trait. This disregards the fact that nature doesn’t dictate what is ‘good’ or ‘bad’, but rather what has helped our ancestors survive. Therefore, the girl is wrong, and being toxic to her boyfriend is not right. Similarly, a man can justify liking and pursuing girls 20 years younger than him because men evolved to look for fertility cues, which younger girls tend to have. This is wrong because usually such an age gap has its own negative implications, and because evolution isn’t a justification for wrongful behavior. 
Understanding these principles has allowed me to reflect on my own experiences with greater nuance. When I feel jealousy or loneliness, I try to adopt an “alien biologist” perspective, as the professor suggested. This mindset fosters curiosity over judgment, allowing me to see these emotions as products of evolutionary pressures without letting them dictate my behavior.
In my daily life, I plan to use this knowledge to create better and stronger connections with others, approaching relationships with more informed expectations. I also hope to continue challenging naturalistic fallacies by separating what is ‘natural’ from what is ethical. By doing so, I hope to learn how to make choices that align with both my evolutionary heritage and my personal values.

Not All The Same

Historically, storytelling—whether through plays, books, movies, or other mediums—has served as a form of entertainment and as a method of imparting life lessons. Think of the stories your family told you growing up, or the lessons found in the Grimm brothers' fairy tales; these narratives are rich with moral teachings passed down through generations. Additionally, think of the thrill of discovering a new favorite movie or binge-watching a compelling TV series, captivated by the intricate plots and characters. This is all to say that all the different stories are valuable to us, as they enrich our understanding of the human condition.

However, this complexity is often oversimplified. Renowned screenwriter and producer John Yorke makes the argument that all stories have the same premise: a “…journey into the woods to find the dark but life-giving secret within” (17) in his book “Into the Woods: A Five-Act Journey Into Story”. For this essay, the interpretation of that quote is that every story has some sort of journey that leads to a discovery that ends up benefitting the characters in some way. I disagree with this assertion because, while stories reduced to the basics might seem similar, this depiction of them doesn’t do justice to their true meaning. This can be illustrated by examining three short stories with a similar premise: “The Lottery” by Shirley Jackson, “The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas”, by Ursula K. LeGuin, and “Rocket Night” by Alexander Weinstein.

To begin with, not all stories have that discovery of the “dark but life-giving secret within” (17), as per Yorke’s argument. “Rocket Night”, a story about an elementary school with a tradition of launching the least liked kid into space, perfectly illustrates this. The darkness of the story isn’t secret; as a matter of fact, it’s revealed in the first sentence when the narrator states that “[i]t was Rocket Night at our daughter’s elementary school… [which meant]... plac[ing] the least-liked child in a rocket and shoot[ing] him into the stars” (Weinstein 1). Also, while the narrator does an amazing job at demonstrating the normalization of this horrible tradition, the story never concretes a meaning, but rather leaves it open for interpretation. Even then, this ‘secret’ isn’t enlightening at all; it’s more of a broad comment on cruelty. There is no “dark but life-giving secret” (Yorke 17); the story just has a dark premise.

Furthermore, reducing stories to their most basic elements, or “boiling them down,” oversimplifies their complexity, which can diminish their significance. By reducing them to the basics, we are stripping them of their intricacy and multidimensionality, which takes away from their depth and meaning. After all, their richness can be found in the nuances and small details. The individuality that this creates is what makes storytelling worthwhile.

This can be illustrated by the stories “The Lottery” by Shirley Jackson, and “The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas”, by Ursula K. LeGuin. “The Lottery” is about a town where they hold a lottery, and the “winner’ gets killed, and “The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas” is about a perfect city that is perfect because of a suffering child. None of the authors reveal why the suffering of one person is needed, instead alluding to its significance throughout the story. In general, they both share a similar concept; a seemingly normal place that sacrifices someone for an unknown reason. Not only that, but they even have a similar structure; starting by describing a nice place, be it a town or a city, and subtly hinting at something dark which isn’t revealed until the end. If boiled down to Yorke’s liking, the takeaway from these stories is society’s acceptance of collective stability being dependent on the suffering of someone. If analyzed comprehensively, though, we get completely different meanings.
In Omelas, people can decide to leave if they can’t stand the idea of a child suffering for the sake of their amazing lives. It isn’t frowned upon, and the only downside the deserters have to face is leaving the beautiful Omelas for the blunt, real world LeGuin simultaneously describes. This makes it clear that most people accept the suffering of the child for their personal benefit, which comments on society's capacity to turn a blind eye to mistreatment if they can reap the benefits. Meanwhile, in “The Lottery”, it’s a collective decision. Either everyone participates, or no one does. But in this town, it isn’t as simple as suggesting the obliteration of the lottery, as it is about respecting tradition and not upsetting the status quo. As illustrated by the following conversation, the option to end this tradition is heavily disliked by the townspeople: “‘They say that over in the north village they’re talking of giving up the lottery.’ Old Man Warner snorted. ‘Pack of crazy fools’...”(Jackson). In turn, this comments on the value that society places on tradition, and how we are prone to blindly follow it simply because “it’s the way it's always been”.

Perhaps what is most interesting about these stories in the face of Yorke’s claim is that none of them have the “journey” that he claims they do. In “The Lottery”, for instance, the plot mostly revolves around the hour before the lottery, but the narration jumps from character to character too quickly to give anyone enough depth. In “The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas”, the narrator just describes Omelas in all its splendor while comparing it to the real world. Finally, in “Rocket Night”, the story is just a nonchalant, impersonal depiction of the tradition. There isn’t any sort of development, be it from the characters or the narration, and most importantly, there isn’t a journey. No one goes through anything to discover the darkness of these societies (especially in “Rocket Night”); the author just outright says so. On top of that, nothing is out of the ordinary for these characters; this is just another lottery, just another day in Omelas, and just another Rocket Night. The richness lies in the peculiarity of these customs and the unique meanings they have. This is different from other stories, where the value can be found in the transformations characters go through in response to the challenges they face, or where change is a vital part of the narrative. 
        
In light of these examples, it becomes clear that stories are far from being “the same”. While patterns and structures are bound to recur, the value of storytelling lies in the diversity of themes, characters, and insights they can provide. Stories like “The Lottery”, “The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas”, and “Rocket Night” challenge simplistic understandings by offering unique insights and structures. If stories truly were all the same, there would be little reason for us to keep consuming them. Yet, we do—because each story brings in a fresh view of the human condition, and an opportunity to see the world through a different lens.

Loneliness, as defined by University of Chicago professors Stephanie and John Caciopopo, “expresses the pain of feeling alone” (Caciopopo et al., 2013). However straightforward it maybe to define on paper, loneliness is an emotion that everyone dreads- but still experiences now and then. Whether it be through ostracism or simply isolation, it creates a sensation of pain that lingers, making its victims feel disconnected from others and from themselves. After experiencing it, it’s easy to wonder why humans were ever meant to feel such a thing, so this essay will examine loneliness as an adaptive motivation system designed to solve challenges in the environment of evolutionary adaptedness (EEA). Further, it will discuss how this system shows evidence of mismatch in modern times.

Let’s start from the beginning. Loneliness likely evolved as a mechanism to encourage social connections when individuals were separated from their group, be it family or any other type of formation. It did (and does) this by “signal[ing] to people that something is wrong concerning their social relationships, and serv[ing] as a motivational force to reestablish these connections”, according to Marlies Maes and Janne Vanhalst from the Department of Interdisciplinary Social Science ad Utrecht University. This makes sense given that being alone was highly dangerous in the ancestral environment, as it meant decreased protection from the environment and less support when finding resources. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that loneliness evolved to address the problem of isolation.

From here, to prove that loneliness is an adaptation, it is important to mention specialized triggers, preparation, behaviors motivated, and cognitive learning programs involved. See, loneliness is specifically triggered by the lack of social connection and interaction, which activates neurobiological responses that then motivate humans to seek social bonds. This shows up as increased surveillance from activating the sympathetic nervous system and decreased immunity, executive functioning, inflammatory control, and sleep quality, (Caciopopo & Boomsma, 2022). Some physical effects, such as the decrease in executive function and sleep quality, signal to the individual that something is wrong, while others, like increased surveillance and activation of the nervous system, prepare the individual to be more aware in social interaction, therefore increasing the probability that it leads to group-formation. Furthermore, cognitive learning programs like increased sensitivity to social cues and hypervigilance to potential social threats guide individuals toward successful social reconnection. This can be seen in action in research by Maner et al. (2007), as it demonstrated that experiences of social exclusion led to increased motivation to form new social bonds. In these experiments, the threat of exclusion led to a heightened desire to make new friends and a greater interest in working together with others, supporting the idea that loneliness or social disconnection motivates reconnection efforts​.

Erika M. Vitale and Adam S. Smith from the department of psychology of the University of Kansas, support this by saying that “social isolation in animal studies leads to increased stress responsiveness and altered motivation, suggesting a deeply ingrained system designed to respond to social threats” (2022). If such a similar mechanism has evolved in other social animals that need to be in groups, we can argue that loneliness is a convergently evolved trait. This would make sense, as again, being in groups is not unique to humans, and it serves the same purpose in all the species it is present in.

As the world is, understandably, no longer what our ancestors evolved in, there is bound to be some mismatch between the current environment and our evolved mechanisms. While our ancestors spent their entire lives together, hunting, living and depending on one another, humans today don’t really rely on others like back then. We work from 9-5, live in one-bedroom apartments, don’t have time for socialization, and replaced reliance on other humans with specialized technologies, like delivery services and Google. Also, while people can now be connected digitally in the form of telecommunication and e-community-building, this type of connection isn’t what our brains seek to fulfill the quota for connection. Therefore, technology is pretty useless in this sense, which is sad considering how easily available it is. Was The Suspect Really Wearing Louboutins?: An Examination of Character Usage Across Different Sources
We’ve all dreamt about being rich and famous, right? If you said no, stop lying. If you said yes, I imagine you understand the appeal of lavish clothes, mansions, and attention from the media. This is especially true in modern times, when we have the best examples of the lifestyles we think we deserve at the tips of our fingers. With a click of a remote or a swipe on a phone screen, we can see what famous people are doing, how, where, and with whom. With such easy access, it’s rare not to fall into the trap of comparison, which can be especially devastating for the ones with the short end of the stick like us. But just how far would you go to be one of them? To dress like them, eat like them, live like them? To answer this question, take a look at this case study.
In 2008, a group of affluent teenagers from Los Angeles stole over 3 million dollars in clothes, bags, weapons, jewelry, and cash from celebrity’s homes. Some of these celebrities included Rachel Bilson, Audrina Partridge, Orlando Bloom, and perhaps most notoriously, Paris Hilton (Sales). When questions in regard to their motives, they all had a cohesive answer: their obsession with celebrities. They admired their lifestyles, mannerisms, styles, and most importantly, their notoriety. 
Ironically enough, by committing these crimes, they became famous too. The best example of this is Alexis Neiers, the daughter of a former Playboy bunny and aspiring model (Sales). Given her unique profile, she was placed front and center in the media coverage, even though she wasn’t as involved as others in the ring. The reasons to why they did this remains unknown, but it has been speculated that outlets used her personal brand to personify the nature of the crimes. This can be clearly evidenced in two of the central media depictions of these crimes: Nancy Jo Sales’ Vanity Fair article "The Suspects Wore Louboutins" and Sofia Coppola’s 2013 film adaptation The Bling Ring. This raises the question: how does the usage of Alexis Neiers as a character affect the narrative surrounding the crimes in the film and article?

In “The Suspects Wore Louboutins”, Alexis Neiers is placed front and center, literally being on the cover page of the article (Sales). The events are mostly narrated through her point of view, mostly in quotations, but Sales constantly diminishes Alexis’s credibility with microaggressions. A great example of this is when the events of the first robbery were being discussed, and Sales quotes Alexis saying “‘[w]hat are you doing? Get me the fuck out of here,’ Neiers said she screamed. Then she went outside and threw up and peed in the bushes” (2010). Instead of simply quoting Alexis, or stating the events, Sales uses a combination of both, with the addition of a ‘said she screamed’. This gives the readers the idea that Alexis’s words are not credible, especially with her state of inebriation being clarified in the next sentence. 
In addition to this, Sales uses specific things that Alexis says to further the idea that she is just a dumb teenager, like when she was quoted saying “God didn’t give me these talents and looks to just sit around being a model or being famous. I want to lead a huge charity organization. I want to lead a country, for all I know” (Sales). This is the only quote like this in the entire article, as no other characters were quoted saying such things, which selectively sheds light on the type of person Alexis is. Moreover, Sales even goes as far as to pit the kid’s words against each other, which can be seen when she quotes Nick Prugo, another one of the suspects, denying Alexis’s first ever statement in the article by saying, “Nick Prugo has a different take on the events of the night of the Bloom burglary. ‘We didn’t even go to Beso that night,’…” (Sales). This, specifically, accomplishes two things: it takes even more credibility from Alexis, and it makes the kids seem disorganized and stupid as a whole. 
Not only that, but Sales uses the acknowledgement of small aesthetic details to further her superficial depiction of Alexis. This can be seen starting from the title of the article, as it emphasizes the kid’s wealth by mentioning a luxury brand. This can also be seen when Sales’ first describes Alexis going into court, saying she was a “A leggy girl with long, dark hair and shimmering blue-green eyes, Neiers was wearing a tweed miniskirt, a pink sweater, and six-inch Christian Louboutin heels” (Sales). In the anniversary article, Sales describes how she mentioned Neiers’s shoes and other luxury items, which she felt were justified in a story centered on celebrity and consumerism (Sales). This approach illustrates how details, like designer shoes, reinforce an image of wealth and superficiality in media, which could supports the idea of the media’s power to shape public perception through specific choices in portrayal. Besides from the fact that this makes Alexis look bad, it was later disproven in a phone call between her and Sales as shown in her show Pretty Wild, where she says that “[Sales] said I was wearing six-inch Louboutins to court with my tweed outfit. I wasn’t wearing Louboutins, I was wearing little brown kitten heels fucking bitch” (Vanity fair, 2013). 
By doing these sorts of things throughout the article, Sales solidifies the idea that Alexis is a spoiled, superficial, dumb teenager. Not only that, but also that Alexis was the front-runner of the ring. In the context of these crimes, being portrayed as superficial, disorganized, and unreliable—as Sales suggests Alexis is—is devastating, as these were precisely the perceptions the kids aimed to counter to mitigate both their social and judicial sentences. David L. Bruce, from the Department of Learning and Instruction at SUNY Buffalo, provides insight on how teenagers are culturally constructed and stereotyped in media, which eerily aligns with Alexis’s case. More specifically, Bruce says that “[m]edia portrayals of adolescents often reflect and reinforce societal stereotypes, reducing them to superficial characteristics that align with cultural constructs of fame, rebellion, and irresponsibility” (Bruce). In the article, Sales’ selective quoting and editorial choices feed into the “spoiled airhead” narrative, further exemplifying Bruce’s point about media’s tendency to oversimplify and stereotype teens.
In the film, however, Alexis isn’t a main character. The plot mostly revolves around Nick and Rachel, their drug use, the reason they commit the crimes, and how they did it. For context, Nick and Rachel, called Marc and Rebecca in the film, were the two ‘ringleaders’, with Rebecca being the one initiating all the robberies, and Nick always standing by her side. In a way, this aligns with the article, as Nick’s point of view is also constantly shared, and their depictions of him align with one another. Alexis’s lack of centrality in the film better reflects the real succession of events, and the fact that the true ringleaders were Nick and Rachel. Alexis, Tess, and the other kids were just tagging along.  This shift in focus from Alexis to Nick and Rachel is crucial to the added depth, as Nick and Rachel’s stories have much more to offer than Alexis’s.
Coppola also constantly makes it known that these crimes were done out of boredom and greed, but that these characters are still people. She does this by highlighting their struggles instead of their flaws. This can be evidenced by the emphasis placed on Mark (Nick)’s ostracism at school and Rebecca (Rachel)’s problems with her parents, and how the characters suffered as a result. In addition to this, the film shows how drugs influenced the crimes, which ended up being a lot, as many of the kids were borderline addicts at the time of the crimes (Sales). 
Moreover, Coppola takes great care in making the film falsely seem superficial, having short clip lengths, accentuating material items, using real name brands, and a painfully 2009’s LA script. But she places this in combination with the demonstrations of the kid’s personal lives and struggles, which effectively make the crimes feel more meaningful than in the article.  This is supported by Sales’ commentary of the film in the 10-year anniversary article titled “Exclusive: Nancy Jo Sales on the 10th Anniversary of the Bling Ring”, saying “[i]t was [not] a shallow film, instead of a film about the shallowness of our era” (Sales). 
These pieces, however different, provide a similar baseline understanding of the crimes to the audience. At the end of the day, there wasn’t really much to it: just a bunch of rich kids getting bored and stealing from celebrities after looking up their information online. Even though Sales’s usage of Alexis gives the crimes a sense of idiocy and superficiality, Coppola’s lack-there-of also accomplishes the same thing, just differently. The film clarifies the idea that while, these robberies were all about celebrity culture and materialism, the people who committed them were still, well, people. This, in turn, slightly changes the tone of these narratives; the article is more bubbly, while the film is much deeper. Subsequently, this changes the ambiance of the crimes. Both the article and the film use Neiers differently to explore themes of fame and materialism, but with distinct tones—Sales presenting her as emblematic of superficiality, and Coppola as part of a larger cultural obsession. While the depiction of the events is pretty much the same in both, this small but significant shift in the film makes it understood that this is more than just a cover story, but a real life succession of events. 
Some can argue that both the article and the film accurately reflect Alexis and the other kids, claiming they embody the stereotype of spoiled, celebrity-obsessed teenagers. They might even say that Sales' portrayal is just honest reporting, showing Alexis as she presented herself: shallow, lacking self-awareness, and materialistic. To them, the film only emphasizes these traits through its aesthetic choices, short clips, and carefully constructed dialogue, reflecting culture rather than a stereotype. If examined through this perspective, Alexis wasn't a victim of media manipulation—she was simply being herself.
However, to accept this argument ignores the specific framing that both Sales and Coppola used to create a specific narrative. Sales chose certain quotes and moments while downplaying other perspectives and critical aspects of Alexis's story. Similarly, Coppola's film, though not centered on Alexis, uses cliched, exaggerated aesthetics to frame the entire group as one-dimensional caricatures of youth, rather than as complex people with motivations and struggles. 
In the end, the portrayals of Alexis Neiers in “The Suspects Wore Louboutins” and “The Bling Ring” reveal how cultural constructs and media choices shape our perceptions of events and of people. Nancy Jo Sales’ article leans into a superficial, critical portrayal, using Alexis as the symbol of shallow, fame-driven youth, while Sofia Coppola’s film subtly explores the underlying social and personal struggles without putting Alexis in the spotlight. These contrasting approaches echo David L. Bruce’s insights on media’s power to reinforce stereotypes, often reducing real people to caricatures to create compelling narratives. By comparing the article’s focus on Alexis’s carefully constructed persona with the film’s broader depiction of teenagers and their angst, we see how these media shapes selectively frame stories to fit cultural expectations.

The person that first comes to mind when someone mentions Colombia (after Medellín’s most notorious ‘businessman’), is Gabriel Garcia Márquez. More specifically, his revered novel, 100 Years of Solitude. 
When I was younger, I refused to read it. I didn’t want to be like the people who read it merely because of its author, and because I wanted to avoid what I assumed was yet another inaccurate representation of my culture. But I was always curious; if there was so much talk surrounding it, there had to be something that made it special. One day, curiosity got the better of me, and I borrowed my mother’s copy. 
As much as I wanted to deny it, the book was a fun read. The storyline was berserk, the characters were indecipherable, and the narrator knew when to make the right remarks. Regardless, I was disappointed by the end. In many ways, it was an inaccurate representation of reality; villages aren’t magical, incest isn’t normal, and no one in their sane mind would name all their family members alike. It almost made up for it with the ‘realism’ parts of its ‘magical realism’ title, with petty feuds that lasted centuries and the profound and doleful effects of armed conflict. But it didn’t. I was expecting a big revelation about ‘The Colombian Identity’ as the critics said it had, but Garcia Márquez left me waiting. 
A few months later, I was in the US when my American friend brought the book up to me when I told her I was Colombian. “Is Colombia like how it is portrayed in the book?” she asked. I was dumbfounded, but just as I was starting to get offended, she cut me off. “I wrote an essay about the portrayal of community in the novel”. Again, I was baffled, except this time, it wasn’t about her ignorance. What did she mean by ‘community’? The relationships between Macondo’s townspeople were pretty normal to me. Sure, they were complex and borderline comical, but how they always are, right? It occurred to me that the dynamics portrayed in the book weren’t standard, as I’d thought. My reality crumbled before me, and it only took a pair of fresh eyes. What else had I missed because of my closed perspective? Since then, I’ve tried to deconstruct everything I deem an absolute given, and promised myself never to fall back into the ‘trap of the single story’ again.
I will always have 100 Years of Solitude to thank for teaching me about the importance of recognizing and questioning our own realities. It's a reminder that, like the intricate tales of Macondo, reality can be both stranger and more magical than we ever imagined. But as we strive to expand our horizons and challenge the single stories that limit our understanding, we can only hope for a more open-minded and empathetic world where diverse perspectives are heard and celebrated.
